question: Under Maryland law, a licensee is subject to discipline for knowingly inducing or attempting to induce someone to sell their home — or discouraging someone from buying a home — by suggesting that a change in the racial, religious, or ethnic makeup of the neighborhood will lower property values, increase crime, or change the character of the neighborhood. This is true even if the licensee gains no money from it. What is this prohibited practice commonly called?
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(16) makes it a ground for discipline to, 'whether or not acting for monetary gain, knowingly induce[] or attempt[] to induce a person to transfer real estate or discourage[] or attempt[] to discourage a person from buying real estate' by representations about the effect on the area of the presence or anticipated presence of persons of a particular race, religion, or national origin. This is the classic 'blockbusting' or 'panic peddling' prohibition, and it applies regardless of whether the licensee profits from it.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(16)

question: A Maryland listing agent tells prospective buyers that anyone who submits an offer this weekend will be entered into a drawing for a free vacation, and separately advertises 'free appraisals' to draw in buyers for a listed property. Under Maryland's licensing statute, this kind of conduct used to influence a party to a real estate sale is:
choice_a: Permitted as long as the drawing is disclosed in writing
choice_b: Permitted only if approved in advance by the Real Estate Commission
choice_c: Permitted because it is a marketing technique, not a misrepresentation
choice_d: A ground for disciplinary action against the licensee
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(9) subjects a licensee to discipline for soliciting, selling, or offering to sell real property so as to influence a prospective party to a sale by offering a prize or free lot, conducting a lottery or contest, or advertising 'free appraisals.' No amount of disclosure or Commission pre-approval makes the practice permissible under this provision.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(9)

question: A Maryland licensee tells a buyer, 'Don't worry about the price — I personally guarantee this house will be worth 20% more when you resell it in five years.' Under Maryland's real estate licensing law, making or authorizing such a guarantee of future resale profits is:
choice_a: A ground for denial, suspension, or revocation of the licensee's license
choice_b: Acceptable puffing that is common in sales talk
choice_c: Acceptable as long as it is put in writing and signed by the buyer
choice_d: Only a problem if the market later declines
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(8) makes it a ground for discipline for a licensee to guarantee, or authorize or allow another person to guarantee, future profits from the resale of real property. It is prohibited outright, not merely conditioned on the accuracy of the prediction or on written disclosure.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(8)

question: A seller has an active exclusive listing contract with Broker A. Broker B contacts the seller directly and urges the seller to cancel that contract and sign a new exclusive listing with Broker B instead. Under Maryland law, Broker B's conduct is:
choice_a: Permitted, since sellers are always free to switch brokers at will
choice_b: A ground for disciplinary action for knowingly soliciting a party to an exclusive listing to terminate it and enter a new contract
choice_c: Permitted only if Broker B first notifies the Real Estate Commission
choice_d: A civil contract matter only, with no licensing consequences
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(12) makes it a ground for discipline for a licensee to 'knowingly solicit[] a party to an exclusive listing contract with another licensee to terminate that contract and enter a new contract.' This directly protects other licensees' existing contractual relationships from being undermined.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(12)

question: Buyer and Seller have already signed a ratified contract of sale that was negotiated through Licensee X. Licensee Y then approaches the buyer and encourages the buyer to breach that contract so the buyer can instead sign a new purchase agreement that Licensee Y negotiates. Under Maryland law, Licensee Y's conduct:
choice_a: Is lawful because the buyer, not Licensee Y, would be the one breaching the contract
choice_b: Is lawful as long as Licensee Y discloses the situation to Licensee X afterward
choice_c: Is a ground for disciplinary action against Licensee Y
choice_d: Only violates the law if Licensee Y is a broker rather than a salesperson
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(13) makes it a ground for discipline for a licensee to solicit a party to a sales contract, lease, or agreement negotiated by another to breach that contract, lease, or agreement in order to substitute a new one. The prohibition applies to the soliciting licensee directly, regardless of who ultimately breaches, and there is no exception for after-the-fact disclosure or for license type.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(13)

question: An associate real estate broker is affiliated with Broker A but begins providing real estate brokerage services on behalf of Broker A in a matter that also involves Broker B, without informing Broker B in writing. Under Maryland's licensing statute, this omission is:
choice_a: Not a licensing issue, since only the associate's own broker (Broker A) needs to be informed
choice_b: Permissible as long as it is disclosed verbally to Broker B at some point
choice_c: Only relevant if Broker B objects to the arrangement
choice_d: A ground for disciplinary action against the associate broker
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(5) makes it a ground for discipline where an associate real estate broker or real estate salesperson provides or attempts to provide real estate brokerage services on behalf of a real estate broker 'without informing in writing any other real estate broker' involved. Written notice to the other broker is required, not merely verbal or after-the-fact disclosure.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(5)

question: A Maryland real estate salesperson is affiliated with Broker A. For a particular transaction, the salesperson accepts a commission directly from Broker C, a broker the salesperson is not affiliated with, rather than having that compensation flow through Broker A. Absent an exception under the compensation statute, this is:
choice_a: A ground for disciplinary action against the salesperson
choice_b: Permitted, since Broker C actually earned the commission being split
choice_c: Permitted as long as Broker A is copied on the check
choice_d: A matter solely between the two brokers, with no effect on the salesperson's license
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(21) makes it a ground for discipline for an associate real estate broker or real estate salesperson to, 'except as provided under § 17-604,' accept a commission or other valuable consideration for real estate brokerage services from any person other than the real estate broker with whom the associate broker or salesperson is affiliated.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(21)

question: A Maryland licensee has actual knowledge that another licensee is violating Title 17 of the Business Occupations and Professions Article in a particular transaction or practice, but continues to associate with that licensee in the same transaction or practice. Under Maryland law, the first licensee's continued association is:
choice_a: Not a violation, because only the licensee who actually breaks the law can be disciplined
choice_b: A ground for disciplinary action, because it constitutes knowingly associating with a violating licensee
choice_c: A violation only if the first licensee personally profits from the misconduct
choice_d: A violation only if the Real Estate Commission has already disciplined the other licensee
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(26) makes it a ground for discipline for a licensee, 'with actual knowledge of the violation,' to associate with a licensee in a transaction or practice that violates any provision of Title 17. Knowing association itself is independently disciplinable, without regard to personal profit or a prior Commission action against the other licensee.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(26)

question: A Maryland licensee is not a member of the local Realtors association, but uses that association's standard contract forms and advertising materials bearing the association's name to make prospective clients believe the licensee belongs to it. Under Maryland's real estate licensing statute, this use of materials naming an organization the licensee does not belong to is:
choice_a: Permitted, since the forms themselves are publicly available
choice_b: Permitted as long as no client specifically asks about membership
choice_c: A ground for disciplinary action against the licensee
choice_d: A copyright issue only, outside the Real Estate Commission's authority
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(17) makes it a ground for discipline for a licensee to use material, including contract forms or advertising matter, that includes the name of an organization or association of which the licensee is not a member. Public availability of the forms and client awareness are not exceptions under the statute.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(17)

question: Beyond the specific prohibited acts it lists, Maryland's real estate licensing statute also allows the Real Estate Commission to discipline a licensee for a broad category of conduct described as demonstrating bad faith, incompetency, or untrustworthiness, or that constitutes dishonest, fraudulent, or improper dealings. This general ethical standard functions as a:
choice_a: Standard that applies only to brokers, never to salespersons or associate brokers
choice_b: Standard enforceable only through a civil lawsuit, not by the Commission
choice_c: Guideline with no actual disciplinary force unless a criminal conviction also results
choice_d: Catch-all ground for discipline covering conduct not necessarily itemized elsewhere in the statute
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(25) authorizes discipline where a licensee 'engages in conduct that demonstrates bad faith, incompetency, or untrustworthiness or that constitutes dishonest, fraudulent, or improper dealings.' This broad, general-ethics provision applies to any licensee under Title 17 and is enforced directly by the Commission, independent of any criminal proceeding.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(25)

question: A Maryland licensee receives a security deposit check from a tenant that belongs to the property owner, but sits on it for weeks without depositing or forwarding it, and does not account for it when asked. Under Maryland's licensing statute, this failure is:
choice_a: A ground for disciplinary action for failing to account for or remit promptly money belonging to another person
choice_b: Not a licensing violation as long as the money is eventually turned over
choice_c: Only a violation if the licensee spends the money personally
choice_d: A matter left entirely to the property owner's civil remedies
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(22) makes it a ground for discipline for a licensee to 'fail[] to account for or to remit promptly any money that comes into the possession of the licensee but belongs to another person.' The duty is to act promptly, so eventual (delayed) turnover does not cure the violation, and the Commission's disciplinary authority exists independent of any civil claim.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(22)

question: A licensee representing a seller learns of a material fact about the property that the licensee knows relates to its condition, but does not disclose it to the buyer, either intentionally or through negligence. Under Maryland's licensing statute, this nondisclosure of a known or knowable material fact is:
choice_a: A violation only if the nondisclosure was intentional
choice_b: A ground for disciplinary action, whether the failure to disclose was intentional or merely negligent
choice_c: A violation only if the buyer can prove financial loss in court
choice_d: Not a licensing issue because sellers, not licensees, owe disclosure duties
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(4) makes it a ground for discipline where a licensee 'intentionally or negligently fails to disclose to any person with whom the...licensee deals a material fact that the licensee knows or should know and that relates to the property.' The statute reaches both intentional and merely negligent nondisclosure, and it applies to the licensee directly.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(4)

question: A Maryland licensee tells a buyer something the licensee knows to be false about a property's condition in order to close the sale. Under Maryland's licensing statute, willfully making such a misrepresentation, or knowingly making a false promise, is:
choice_a: A violation only if the statement is put in writing
choice_b: A violation only if the buyer relied on the statement and suffered damages
choice_c: A ground for disciplinary action against the licensee
choice_d: Treated the same as an honest mistake about the property
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(3) makes it a ground for discipline where a licensee, 'directly or through another person, willfully makes a misrepresentation or knowingly makes a false promise.' The provision targets willful or knowing conduct rather than honest error, and it does not require proof of the buyer's reliance or damages for the Commission to act.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(3)

question: A Maryland broker wants to avoid paying a full commission to a licensed salesperson, so the broker instead retains an unlicensed individual to perform the same brokerage functions, specifically to get around the law prohibiting payment of a commission to an unlicensed person. Under Maryland's licensing statute, retaining an unlicensed individual for this purpose is:
choice_a: Permitted as long as the unlicensed individual is called an 'assistant' rather than a salesperson
choice_b: Permitted if the unlicensed individual is a family member of the broker
choice_c: Only a tax issue, not a licensing issue
choice_d: A ground for disciplinary action against the broker
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(7) makes it a ground for discipline where a licensee 'retains or attempts to retain the services of any unlicensed individual as an associate real estate broker or a real estate salesperson to evade the law prohibiting payment of a commission' to an unlicensed person. Relabeling the role or the individual's relationship to the broker does not avoid the violation.
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-322(b)(7)

question: A Maryland real estate broker has several affiliated salespersons and independent contractors working under the broker's license. Under Maryland law, what is the broker's ethical and statutory obligation regarding these individuals' provision of real estate brokerage services?
choice_a: The broker must exercise reasonable and adequate supervision over the brokerage services provided on the broker's behalf, regardless of how the individual is affiliated
choice_b: The broker has no supervisory duty over independent contractors, only over salaried employees
choice_c: Supervision is required only if a client specifically requests it
choice_d: The duty to supervise applies only during the first year after a salesperson is licensed
explanation: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. § 17-320(c) requires that 'a real estate broker shall exercise reasonable and adequate supervision over the provision of real estate brokerage services by any other individual, including an independent contractor, on behalf of the broker,' and this duty applies regardless of how the individual is affiliated with the broker. Failing this supervisory duty is itself a separate ground for discipline under § 17-322(b)(27).
source_note: Md. Code Ann., Bus. Occ. & Prof. §§ 17-320(c), 17-322(b)(27)
